title: AI Encounters of the Dubious Kind: Bjork, Generative Learning and the Need to Think for Yourself d-the-need-to-think-for-yourself/
author: Sherrington, Tom
summary: Tom Sherrington uses a live classroom moment—asking ChatGPT about 'the Bjorks' redundancy effect' and receiving a confident, entirely fabricated explanation—to illustrate two risks: AI's scarily convincing expression of false certainty, and the meta-risk that only someone who already knows the field can catch the error. A student novice would not know to push back. He then summarizes what he describes as ChatGPT's own research summary on AI and cognitive offloading—noting, after the fact, that he did none of the thinking required to generate or evaluate it himself—as a demonstration of the very problem under discussion. Three student use cases follow (knowledge-product homework, AI-generated bee-pollination posters, feedback on student writing) each illustrating how AI can produce superficially impressive outputs while bypassing the thinking that is the actual learning goal. Sherrington's conclusion: generative learning processes must be actively protected. AI can be a prompt to support self-explaining and self-testing, but wherever AI stops students from thinking, summarizing, and imagining, learning is impeded.
points: Only the knowledgeable can catch AI's confident errors. Sherrington could identify the hallucinated 'Bjork redundancy effect' because he had prior knowledge of the Bjorks' actual research. A student novice doing the same search would not notice. This is the deepest structural problem for AI use in learning: the very people who most need the tool are the least equipped to detect when it is confidently wrong.

AI fundamentally breaks knowledge-product homework as a valid learning process. When a student can produce a polished poster on bee pollination without doing any biological thinking, the homework has been completed in form but bypassed in substance. Teachers need to design tasks that require thinking AI cannot perform on the student's behalf.

The delegation loop is a self-reinforcing risk: as AI gets better, people delegate more; as they delegate more, their thinking capacity weakens; as capacity weakens, they rely on AI even more. This is the strongest emerging concern about AI's long-term effect on independent cognition.

AI feedback on student writing opens genuine possibilities: students who write authentically can get useful, rapid feedback without needing teacher availability. The hard part is ensuring the initial work is genuinely the student's before the feedback loop begins.
quotes: The point here is that I could only notice that the response was wildly wrong because I already have knowledge that helps me notice and redirect the enquiries. If I was a student novice doing a search I might not notice at all.

I have a list of six categories I didn't create and it's not formed coherent schema in my mind at all. This is the big big risk to students using AI for their learning if they do not need to routinely engage in the heavy lifting required to do this kind of thinking on their own.
AI fundamentally destroys creating knowledge product homeworks as a valid learning process because no thinking is needed to make them. We're going to need alternatives.

Where AI stop students thinking, summarising, mapping, imagining etc - we are impeding their learning. However AI could be a prompt to support self-explaining, hearing students engage in teaching, checking the accuracy of their summaries and self-testing.
Authentic generative learning that demands using our own knowledge must be at the front and centre of how we construct teaching, curriculum and assessment.
